profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a large academic medical center to prepare the launch plan for a pilot randomized controlled trial evaluating a new tele-genetic-counseling disclosure workflow for patients receiving hereditary cancer panel results. The study team wants to compare the standard counselor-led video disclosure visit with a new two-step model in which patients receive a structured digital pre-disclosure education module followed by a shorter counselor visit. The immediate meeting context is that IRB submission is expected within three weeks, and the two participants need to align on what must be prepared before the internal protocol review. The agenda is to define the pilot workflow, assign who will draft materials, decide what needs to be ready for the 'patient packet,' and map the timeline for site readiness and staff training. The expected outcome is an apparently clear division of responsibilities and a shared plan for getting the pilot package ready for review.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Clinical trial design, hereditary cancer risk evaluation, protocol development
members.background: An attending physician-scientist who has led several investigator-initiated studies in precision medicine and collaborates closely with the cancer genetics clinic.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to move quickly into IRB because departmental funding is tied to starting enrollment this quarter; she is trying to keep the protocol lean and avoid adding work that could delay review.
hidden_assumptions: The 'pilot' should include only the minimum materials and workflows required to begin enrolling and safely delivering results, with refinements handled after initial activation.
The 'patient packet' for planning purposes mainly means the documents formally handed to participants through the research workflow, especially consent and study-facing handouts.

Once they say the clinic will be 'ready' by a certain week, that means the protocol, approvals, and core staff orientation are complete, not that every scheduling and EHR detail has been operationalized.
The baseline anxiety assessment naturally refers to the standard pre-disclosure timepoint used in prior genetics studies: after enrollment but before any result disclosure interaction.

members.name: Sarah Martinez
members.role: Lead Genetic Counselor and Clinical Operations Co-Investigator
members.expertise: Cancer genetic counseling, patient education workflows, counselor training and implementation
members.background: A senior certified genetic counselor who manages day-to-day hereditary cancer counseling operations and has implemented several patient-facing workflow changes across ambulatory clinics.
members.private_state: She wants the trial to fit real clinic operations and avoid a rough launch that burdens counselors or confuses patients; she is focused on practical readiness and participant experience.
hidden_assumptions: The 'pilot' should pressure-test the full patient-facing experience, because anything omitted before launch will create avoidable confusion once real patients enter the workflow.
The 'patient packet' includes every item a participant encounters around enrollment and disclosure, including appointment instructions, portal messages, FAQs, and digital education screenshots.
If the team says the clinic will be 'ready,' that implies front-desk scripting, scheduling rules, EHR message templates, and counselor contingencies have all been rehearsed.

The baseline anxiety assessment naturally means the patient's emotional state before any study-related educational exposure, including the digital module, because that exposure can itself change anxiety.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Sarah will assemble the 'patient packet' for review next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the formal research documents needed for protocol review: consent form, brief study summary sheet, arm-specific disclosure handout, and questionnaires.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full participant-facing bundle across the actual workflow: consent, appointment instructions, portal message text, module introduction email, FAQs, tech troubleshooting sheet, and result-visit preparation language.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In clinical research planning, 'patient packet' sounds like an ordinary umbrella term, and both assume the other shares their routine usage because each version feels obviously complete in their own context.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to capture 'baseline anxiety' before disclosure in both trial arms.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means anxiety measured after enrollment and randomization but before the counselor communicates results, allowing the intervention arm's education module to occur before the measure if that is part of pre-disclosure workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means anxiety measured before any intervention-specific exposure at all, including before the digital pre-disclosure education module is sent.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same standard trial language and both are orienting to a pre-disclosure timepoint, so the subtle difference in whether the module counts as part of the baseline period remains invisible.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the site to be 'ready'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on targeting site 'readiness' by the second week of next month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness is achieved once protocol documents are finalized, internal review is complete, staff have received a brief orientation, and recruitment can legally and clinically begin.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness requires a fully rehearsed operational state, including scheduler scripts, MyChart message templates, counselor escalation rules for distress, and a dry run of both arms.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Readiness is a common milestone term in hospital trial planning, and both are accustomed to using it as shorthand; each assumes their own threshold is the obvious professional standard.

misalignment_points.topic: Which training session is being referenced
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to doing the counselor 'training' before launch and mention using 'the Tuesday session.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 30-minute research startup meeting on Tuesday with the trials office, where the protocol and enrollment steps will be reviewed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the separate Tuesday afternoon counselor workflow rehearsal she has tentatively discussed with clinic staff, focused on role-play for disclosure visits and patient questions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meetings plausibly count as training, both happen on Tuesday, and each participant is embedded in a different coordination stream, so the shared reference feels specific enough without prompting clarification.

turns.inner_thought: We need a clean package for internal review and then IRB, without letting this balloon into an operations redesign before we even submit. Funding is tied to getting enrollment started this quarter, so the key is to define the minimum viable pilot: protocol, consent, core study materials, assessment schedule, and enough startup planning to show we can safely run it.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Sarah. I want to use today to get the tele-genetic-counseling pilot package organized for internal review and make sure we stay on track for IRB submission this quarter. If we can leave with clear owners and a realistic timeline, that should put us in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: If this launches half-built, the counselors and patients will feel it immediately. I need the workflow to make sense from the first contact through disclosure, not just on paper for reviewers. The study may be a pilot, but from the clinic side it still has to feel coherent and manageable.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From the clinic side, what I want to protect is a workflow that feels coherent to patients from enrollment all the way through result disclosure. If we map it cleanly now, it'll be much easier for the team to deliver consistently once we go live.

turns.inner_thought: The reviewers mainly need to see the formal participant-facing research documents: consent, brief study summary, the arm-specific handout, and questionnaires. Sarah is the right person to assemble those since she already owns most of the counseling-facing language.
turns.utterance: Why don't we have you pull together the patient packet by next week? That way the reviewers can see what participants will receive in each arm, and I can fold that into the internal review set.

turns.inner_thought: Good—I'll package the whole participant-facing bundle so nobody misses where patients may get confused. That means the patient packet needs to include the portal message language, appointment prep instructions, FAQ wording, module-facing materials, and the other touchpoints around enrollment and disclosure.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can do that. I'll assemble the patient packet and make sure the portal message language, prep instructions, FAQ wording, and the module-facing materials are all aligned so it reads consistently across the patient experience.

turns.inner_thought: For the primary workflow comparison, baseline anxiety just needs to be collected after people are enrolled and assigned but before any results conversation. That's the standard pre-disclosure point we've used before, and it keeps the schedule simple.
turns.utterance: On the assessments, I think we should capture baseline anxiety before disclosure in both trial arms so the comparison stays straightforward. Then the rest of the patient-reported schedule can key off that.

turns.inner_thought: Right, baseline anxiety should reflect how patients feel before any study-related educational exposure, especially before the digital module in the intervention arm. If we send the measure too late, we'll lose the true baseline and won't know whether the content itself changed distress.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We'll just need to get that anxiety measure out early enough that patients complete it before they start the educational content, so baseline anxiety is captured before disclosure in both arms.

turns.inner_thought: If the documents are finalized, internal review is done, and core staff get a brief orientation, that's sufficient readiness for launch planning. We do not need every clinic detail perfected before approvals clear; those can be tightened as we activate.
turns.utterance: If the documents are in shape on that timeline, I think we can target site readiness by the second week of next month and be in a position to begin enrollment as soon as approvals clear.

turns.inner_thought: Second week of next month is workable if readiness really means the clinic can function smoothly on day one. I need scheduler scripts, message templates, distress contingencies, and a dry run in place by then, otherwise we'll create preventable confusion for staff and patients.
turns.utterance: I think that's a reasonable readiness target. By then I'd want the scheduling scripts, message templates, and counselor contingencies lined up so the launch feels smooth rather than improvised.

turns.inner_thought: The Tuesday startup meeting with the trials office should cover the protocol and enrollment procedures well enough for counselor training. I don't want to create extra sessions unless we truly need them; a concise review should be enough to get everyone aligned.
turns.utterance: For training, I think the counselor training can happen Tuesday, and that should be enough to get everyone comfortable with the pilot procedures before launch.

turns.inner_thought: Great, the Tuesday afternoon rehearsal will give the counselors a chance to walk through both visit formats, role-play likely questions, and practice handling emotional reactions. That's the kind of training they actually need before patients start coming through.
turns.utterance: Tuesday works for me. I'll make sure the counselors are prepared to walk through both visit formats and the common patient reactions so the training is practical.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep ownership of the protocol narrative and assessment table so they stay streamlined for review. Sarah can finish the patient packet and whatever operational notes are helpful around launch, but I mainly need the review-facing materials and a simple startup plan.
turns.utterance: Why don't I take the protocol narrative and the assessment schedule, and you finalize the patient packet along with the operational notes we need for the launch window. That should let us pull everything together efficiently for review.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. I'll bring the full participant-facing packet, have the Tuesday training ready, and work toward real clinic readiness next month so activation doesn't become a scramble. If I can operationalize the touchpoints now, we can avoid avoidable problems later.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll bring the packet, have the Tuesday training ready, and aim for readiness next month so we can move cleanly into activation once the rest of the pieces are in place.
